Neuron: cell body.description: The cell body, or soma, contains the nucleus and the protein-making machinery of the cell. It integrates the signals arriving from the dendrites, and the impulse is usually started just beyond it, at the axon hillock and initial segment.
clinical: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, motor neurons whose cell bodies lie in the motor cortex, brainstem and spinal cord gradually die. This causes progressive muscle weakness and wasting.

Neuron: soma organelles.description: The rough ER, studded with ribosomes, appears as Nissl substance, which stains strongly in lab slides, and it makes membrane and secreted proteins. The Golgi apparatus packages and sorts these proteins, and the mitochondria make most of the cell's energy as ATP.
clinical: Chromatolysis after axon injury

When an axon is cut, the cell body often swells and its Nissl substance breaks up, a change called chromatolysis. This is thought to reflect a shift of the neuron's protein-making machinery toward repairing the damaged axon.
Mitochondrial disease

Mitochondrial diseases, caused by faults in the energy-making machinery of mitochondria, often affect the brain, nerves and muscles. These tissues depend heavily on energy supply, so they are commonly affected.

Neuron: dendrites and axon.description: Dendrites are branching processes that receive signals from other neurons and carry them toward the cell body. The axon is a single long process that carries impulses away from the cell body, and it ends in terminals (boutons) that pass the signal on to the next cell.
clinical: Diabetic neuropathy
The longest axons, such as those running to the feet, are usually damaged first. In diabetic neuropathy this causes numbness, tingling and pain that start in the toes and feet.
Alzheimer disease
Loss of dendritic spines, the small bumps on dendrites that receive synapses, is an early change in Alzheimer disease. This loss is thought to contribute to memory problems.

Neuron: myelin.description: Myelin is a fatty insulating wrap made of many layers of glial cell membrane around the axon. Oligodendrocytes make it in the brain and spinal cord, and Schwann cells make it in peripheral nerves. Because it lets the impulse jump between nodes, conduction is much faster.
clinical: Multiple sclerosis
In multiple sclerosis the immune system attacks myelin in the brain and spinal cord, leaving scarred patches called plaques. The damaged areas slow or block nerve signals.
Guillain-Barré syndrome
In the common form of Guillain-Barré syndrome the immune system attacks the myelin of peripheral nerves, often after an infection. The resulting weakness typically spreads over days.

Neuron: nodes of Ranvier.description: Nodes of Ranvier are short gaps between the myelin segments of an axon, where the axon membrane is bare. Voltage-gated sodium channels cluster here, so the action potential is regenerated at each node and appears to jump from node to node. This jumping, called saltatory conduction, makes signals travel much faster than along an unmyelinated axon.
clinical: Acute motor axonal neuropathy

In acute motor axonal neuropathy, a form of Guillain-Barré syndrome, antibodies attack the axon membrane at the nodes of Ranvier and damage motor nerves directly. This causes weakness that can develop over days.

Neuron: node sodium channels.description: Voltage-gated sodium channels cluster at each node of Ranvier. When the membrane depolarises they open and let sodium in, regenerating the action potential so the signal reaches the next node.
clinical: Local anaesthetics
Local anaesthetics such as lidocaine block these sodium channels. Blocking them stops impulses in that nerve, which is how a numbing injection works.
Pufferfish poison
Tetrodotoxin, a toxin found in pufferfish, blocks the same channels. It can cause paralysis because nerve impulses can no longer be generated.

Node detail: sodium channels.description: NaV1.6 is one of the main sodium channels at the node of Ranvier. Its large alpha subunit forms the pore through the membrane, and a smaller beta1 subunit helps anchor the channel at the node.
clinical: SCN8A epilepsy
Mutations in SCN8A, the gene that encodes this channel, can cause severe early-onset epilepsy with developmental delay.

Node detail.description: A node of Ranvier is packed with sodium channels, and its membrane is supported by a scaffold of spectrin and actin, which ankyrin-G links to the channels. On each side the myelin ends in paranodal loops that seal against the axon and keep the channels confined to the node.

Synapse: membranes.description: A synapse is the junction where one neuron passes a signal to another. The presynaptic side is the membrane of the axon terminal, the postsynaptic side is the membrane of a dendritic spine, and a narrow gap called the synaptic cleft separates them.

Synapse: bouton contents.description: The axon terminal, or bouton, is packed with synaptic vesicles filled with neurotransmitter. Mitochondria supply the energy for recycling vesicles and pumping calcium, and motor proteins carry cargo such as vesicles and mitochondria along microtubules to the terminal.

Synapse: release site.description: At the active zone, synaptic vesicles dock against the presynaptic membrane, held by protein tethers and ready to fuse. When a vesicle fuses with the membrane it releases its glutamate into the synaptic cleft, where it can reach receptors on the other side.
clinical: Botulinum toxin

Botulinum toxin, made by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum, cuts the SNARE proteins that let vesicles fuse, so the nerve cannot release its transmitter. This paralyses muscle, and purified forms are used medically to relax overactive muscles.

Synapse: calcium channels.description: These are N-type (CaV2.2) voltage-gated calcium channels in the presynaptic membrane, clustered at the active zone. When an action potential arrives, calcium flows in through them and triggers synaptic vesicles to fuse and release their transmitter.
clinical: Gabapentin and pregabalin

These drugs, used for nerve pain and epilepsy, bind to the α2δ subunit of these channels. This reduces the number of channels reaching the membrane, so less calcium enters and less transmitter is released.
Ziconotide
Ziconotide, a peptide from cone snail venom, blocks N-type calcium channels. It is given into the spinal fluid to treat severe chronic pain.

Synapse: postsynaptic side.description: The postsynaptic density is a thick protein scaffold under the postsynaptic membrane that holds the receptors opposite the release site. Actin filaments in the spine shape its head and neck, and these change as synapses strengthen or weaken.
clinical: Phelan-McDermid syndrome

SHANK3 is a major scaffold protein of the postsynaptic density. Losing one working copy of its gene, usually through a deletion at the end of chromosome 22 (22q13), causes Phelan-McDermid syndrome, with intellectual disability, delayed speech and autism-like features.

Synapse: AMPA receptors.description: AMPA receptors are glutamate-gated channels in the postsynaptic membrane and are the main fast excitatory receptors in the brain. Each receptor is built from four subunits, such as GluA2, and when glutamate binds the channel opens to let sodium in, depolarising the spine.
clinical: Stroke and excitotoxicity

After a stroke, too much glutamate is released and overactivates glutamate receptors, including AMPA receptors. The excess calcium and sodium entry injures and kills neurons, a process called excitotoxicity.

parts.description: Dendrites are the branching processes that extend from the cell body and receive most of the synaptic input from other neurons. They taper as they branch and carry these signals inwards toward the cell body. In a stained histological section, the thicker proximal dendrites still contain Nissl substance (clusters of rough endoplasmic reticulum), which fades out in the finer distal branches, and many small dendritic spines dot their surface.

The axon hillock is the cone-shaped region of the cell body where the axon leaves the soma. It has a high density of voltage-gated sodium channels (which open when the membrane voltage changes) and forms part of the trigger zone where action potentials usually begin. In a stained section it looks like a pale, tapering cone free of Nissl substance (clustered rough ER), which makes it easy to pick out.

The axon initial segment is the short stretch of axon that runs from the axon hillock until the myelin begins. It is packed with voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels (which open when the membrane voltage changes), anchored by a scaffolding protein called ankyrin-G, and it is where action potentials are normally generated. Because it is usually unmyelinated and free of Nissl substance (clustered rough ER), it looks like a plain, narrow stretch between the cell body and the first myelin segment.

The axon is the single long process of a neuron that carries impulses away from the cell body toward its target. It starts at the axon hillock, usually keeps a uniform diameter and gives off side branches called collaterals, and it is often wrapped in myelin to speed conduction. In a stained section it looks paler than the cell body, because the cell body is packed with Nissl substance (clustered rough ER) and the axon is not.

Axon terminals are the branched endings of an axon, where the neuron releases its neurotransmitter to pass the signal on to the next cell. Each small swelling along these branches is a bouton (also called a varicosity), and each bouton usually contains synaptic vesicles and mitochondria. In stained preparations the terminals look like a string of beads along the fine end branches of the axon.

The neuronal cell body, or perikaryon, is the expanded part of the neuron that surrounds the nucleus and holds most of the cell's organelles. Its cytoplasm is rich in rough endoplasmic reticulum, which forms Nissl substance and stains strongly with basic dyes such as cresyl violet. In a stained section the cell body appears as a large, rounded profile filled with basophilic granules, which sets it apart from the thinner processes that leave it.

The outer nuclear membrane is the outer of the two lipid bilayers that form the nuclear envelope, which separates the nucleus from the cytoplasm. Its outer face is studded with ribosomes and is continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum, whose lumen opens into the gap between the two nuclear membranes. In an electron micrograph it appears as the outer of two dark lines, with a pale perinuclear space between them.

The inner nuclear membrane is the inner of the two membranes that make up the nuclear envelope, and it faces the nucleoplasm, the fluid inside the nucleus. It is lined by the nuclear lamina, a meshwork of lamin filaments (a type of intermediate filament) that gives the nucleus its shape and anchors chromatin to the envelope. In an electron micrograph it is the inner dark line of the envelope, and dense, tightly packed heterochromatin is often seen pressed against it.

The nucleolus is a dense, membrane-free region inside the nucleus where ribosomal RNA is made and ribosome subunits are assembled. It forms around clusters of ribosomal RNA genes on several chromosomes, and it is usually the most conspicuous body within the nucleus. Neurons have large nucleoli because they make so much protein, and in a stained section it shows as a dark round spot inside the pale nucleus.

The rough endoplasmic reticulum is a network of flattened membrane sacs studded with ribosomes on their outer surface, and it makes membrane and secreted proteins. In a neuron it is abundant in the cell body and proximal dendrites, where it forms Nissl substance. Nissl substance appears as basophilic granular clumps that stain strongly with basic dyes such as cresyl violet, and it is absent from the axon hillock and most of the axon.

Ribosomes on the rough ER are the protein-making particles that sit on the outer face of its membranes, each built from ribosomal RNA and protein in large and small subunits. Those bound to the rough ER make proteins destined for membranes, lysosomes or secretion, while free ribosomes in the cytosol make proteins that stay in the cell. In an electron micrograph they appear as small dark dots lining the ER membranes, and their RNA is what makes Nissl substance so basophilic.

The Golgi apparatus is a stack of flattened membrane sacs (cisternae) beside the nucleus, and it receives newly made proteins from the rough ER. It modifies these proteins, for example by adding sugar groups, and sorts them into vesicles for delivery to the cell surface, lysosomes or secretion. It can be shown in neurons by silver staining, where it appears as a dark, net-like mass beside the nucleus.

Golgi transport vesicles are small membrane-bound carriers that bud off from the edges of the Golgi cisternae. They carry proteins and lipids from the Golgi to the cell surface, to lysosomes and to the dendrites and axon, moving along microtubules with motor proteins. They are far too small to see with a light microscope, so in practice they are recognised only in electron micrographs as small round profiles clustered near the Golgi.

The outer mitochondrial membrane is the smooth outer boundary of a mitochondrion, enclosing the intermembrane space and the folded inner membrane. It contains porin proteins, such as VDAC (voltage-dependent anion channel), that let small molecules pass freely, so it is far more permeable than the inner membrane. It also makes contact with the endoplasmic reticulum at sites where calcium and lipids are exchanged. In an electron micrograph it appears as the smooth, continuous outer line of the organelle.

keys: Cell body mitochondrion 1: inner membrane and cristae
Cell body mitochondrion 2: inner membrane and cristae
parts.description: The inner mitochondrial membrane is the folded membrane inside a mitochondrion, and it is almost impermeable to ions. It holds the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, which together make most of the cell's ATP by oxidative phosphorylation. Its infoldings, called cristae, greatly increase the surface area for this process. In an electron micrograph the cristae show as folds of dark membrane projecting into the matrix, the inner compartment.

The α subunit of a voltage-gated sodium channel (a channel that opens when the membrane voltage changes) is the large, pore-forming protein that lets sodium ions pass through the axon membrane. It is built from four homologous domains, each with six membrane-spanning segments, and its voltage-sensing segments move when the membrane depolarises (becomes less negative), opening the pore. At the nodes of Ranvier this subunit allows the rapid sodium influx that regenerates the action potential.

The β1 subunit is a smaller auxiliary protein that associates with the large α subunit of a sodium channel but does not form the pore itself. It tunes how quickly the channel opens and inactivates, helps the α subunit reach the membrane, and its outer immunoglobulin-like domain (a folded, antibody-like region) lets the channel adhere to neighbouring cell-surface molecules.

keys: Node detail: NaV1.6 channel 1, α subunit
Node detail: NaV1.6 channel 2, α subunit
Node detail: NaV1.6 channel 3, α subunit
parts.description: The α subunit of NaV1.6 is the large, pore-forming part of this sodium channel. NaV1.6 is the main variant (isoform) of the sodium channel at mature nodes of Ranvier, so this subunit carries most of the sodium current that drives the nodal action potential. Its central pore lets sodium through when the channel opens, and tetrodotoxin, a toxin from pufferfish, binds to this subunit to block the pore.

keys: Node detail: NaV1.6 channel 1, β1 subunit
Node detail: NaV1.6 channel 2, β1 subunit
Node detail: NaV1.6 channel 3, β1 subunit
parts.description: The β1 subunit of NaV1.6 is a small auxiliary protein that sits alongside the large α subunit and does not form the pore. It alters how quickly the channel opens and inactivates and helps the α subunit reach the membrane. Its outer immunoglobulin-like domain (a folded, antibody-like region) lets it adhere to neighbouring molecules, which helps keep the channels in their dense cluster at the node.

keys: Node detail: axon membrane at the node
parts.description: The axon membrane at the node of Ranvier is the bare patch of the axon's plasma membrane where the myelin sheath is absent. It is a lipid bilayer with a very high density of voltage-gated sodium channels (which open when the membrane voltage changes), far higher than along the myelinated internode, which is why the action potential is regenerated here. In an electron micrograph the node looks like a short gap in the dark myelin, with the axon's own membrane exposed to the extracellular fluid.

The paranode is the region at each end of a myelin internode, beside a node of Ranvier, where the myelin sheath ends in spiralling loops called paranodal loops. These loops attach to the axon through specialised septate-like junctions, which seal the nodal region and keep the sodium channels confined to the node. In an electron micrograph the paranode shows as the place where the myelin turns back on itself and tapers down onto the axon.

The spectrin–actin undercoat is the cytoskeletal lattice lying just beneath the axon membrane at a node of Ranvier. βIV-spectrin, a long, flexible protein, links to short actin filaments (thin protein strands) to form a mesh that supports the membrane and holds the channels in a tight cluster. This mesh is tied to the sodium channels through ankyrin-G, which binds both the channels and the spectrin.

Ankyrin-G is a scaffolding protein that links the sodium channels at a node of Ranvier to the spectrin–actin lattice beneath the membrane. It binds the intracellular loops of the sodium channel α subunit and βIV-spectrin, so the channels are clustered and held in place. Without ankyrin-G, sodium channels fail to gather at the nodes, and conduction along the axon becomes unreliable.

The presynaptic membrane is the membrane of the axon terminal, or bouton, that faces the synaptic cleft and is the site of transmitter release. It contains the active zone, a specialised patch where voltage-gated calcium channels (which open when the membrane depolarises) cluster and synaptic vesicles dock and fuse. Calcium entering through these channels triggers the vesicles to release their transmitter into the cleft; in an electron micrograph the active zone shows as a dense band on the inner face of the membrane.

The bouton membrane is the plasma membrane that encloses the whole bouton, the small swelling at the end of an axon branch, and it is continuous with the membrane of the axon. It encloses the synaptic vesicles, mitochondria and cytoskeleton, separating them from the extracellular space. In an electron micrograph the bouton is recognised as a swelling packed with small clear vesicles and bounded by one continuous membrane.

keys: Synapse: dendritic spine and shaft membrane
parts.description: The postsynaptic membrane is the plasma membrane of a dendritic spine and of the adjacent dendritic shaft, facing the synaptic cleft. It carries glutamate receptors, including AMPA receptors, which open their channels as soon as glutamate binds, and NMDA receptors, which also need the membrane to be depolarised before they pass current. In silver-stained preparations, spines look like small knobs or thorns on the surface of a dendrite.

keys: Synapse: spine membrane cut edge, outer head groups
parts.description: The outer head groups are the water-attracting (hydrophilic) ends of the phospholipids that form the outer layer of the dendritic spine's plasma membrane, facing the synaptic cleft. Each phospholipid has a phosphate-containing head and two fatty acid tails, and these heads point outwards into the extracellular fluid. Their attraction to water keeps the membrane stable by holding the water-repelling tails safely inside. On an electron micrograph this layer shows as one of the two dark lines of the membrane's three-layered profile.

keys: Synapse: spine membrane cut edge, fatty core
parts.description: The fatty core is the water-repelling (hydrophobic) middle of the dendritic spine membrane, formed by the fatty acid tails of the phospholipids packed tail to tail. This central zone keeps charged ions and water-soluble molecules from crossing the membrane freely, which is what makes the membrane a barrier. On an electron micrograph it appears as a pale band between the two dark head-group lines.

keys: Synapse: spine membrane cut edge, inner head groups
parts.description: The inner head groups are the polar heads of the phospholipids in the inner layer of the dendritic spine membrane, facing the cytoplasm inside the spine. Some of these heads carry phosphoinositides such as PIP2, a signalling lipid that binds cytoskeletal proteins and helps anchor the membrane to the actin cytoskeleton. Like the outer heads, they show as a dark line on an electron micrograph.

keys: Synapse: calcium channel A, α1 pore
Synapse: calcium channel B, α1 pore
parts.description: The α1 pore subunit is the large core protein of the N-type (CaV2.2) calcium channel and forms the channel's calcium-selective pore and voltage sensor. It is built from four similar domains, each with six membrane-spanning helices, which arrange around a central pore that passes through the presynaptic membrane. When an action potential depolarises the terminal, the voltage sensor moves, the pore opens and calcium flows into the axon terminal to trigger vesicle fusion.

keys: Synapse: calcium channel A, α2δ-1 subunit
Synapse: calcium channel B, α2δ-1 subunit
parts.description: The α2δ-1 subunit is an auxiliary (helper) subunit of the calcium channel, made of an extracellular α2 part linked by a disulphide bond to a membrane-anchored δ part. It helps the pore-forming α1 subunit reach the presynaptic membrane and increases the current the channel carries. It is also the binding site for the drugs gabapentin and pregabalin, which are used to treat neuropathic pain and epilepsy.

keys: Synapse: calcium channel A, β3 subunit
Synapse: calcium channel B, β3 subunit
parts.description: The β3 subunit is an intracellular (inside the cell) auxiliary (helper) subunit of the calcium channel, lying on the inner face of the presynaptic membrane. It binds the loop joining the first two domains of the pore-forming α1 subunit, helping the channel reach the membrane and open and close with the right timing.

parts.description: The GluA2 subunit is one of the four protein chains that assemble to form an AMPA receptor, the main fast excitatory glutamate-gated channel in the brain. Each subunit has a glutamate-binding domain that clamps shut around glutamate, and this movement pulls open the channel gate in the membrane. RNA editing of the pore loop changes one amino acid, glutamine to arginine, which makes receptors containing the edited subunit impermeable to calcium.

Stargazin is a transmembrane AMPA receptor regulatory protein (TARP), an auxiliary subunit that associates with AMPA receptors and helps traffic them into the synapse. It has four membrane-spanning segments and a tail that binds PSD-95, a scaffold protein, anchoring the receptor at the postsynaptic density. It also slows the receptor's desensitisation and boosts its current.

The outer membrane is the smooth, continuous outer wall of a mitochondrion in the axon terminal, separating the organelle from the surrounding cytoplasm. It contains voltage-dependent anion channels (VDAC), porin channels that let small molecules and ions pass freely, so the space between the two membranes is chemically close to the cytoplasm. On an electron micrograph it appears as a smooth outline, unlike the folded inner membrane.

keys: Synapse: bouton mitochondrion, inner membrane and cristae
parts.description: The inner membrane is the folded membrane inside a mitochondrion, forming shelf-like cristae that greatly increase its surface area. It carries the electron transport chain, a series of respiratory enzymes, and the enzyme ATP synthase, which together make ATP by oxidative phosphorylation to power vesicle recycling and calcium pumping. In an electron micrograph the cristae show as inward folds inside a smooth outer outline.

Axonal microtubules are hollow tubes about 25 nm wide, built from α- and β-tubulin dimers arranged in 13 chains called protofilaments. They run the length of the axon with their plus ends pointing towards the terminal, forming tracks along which kinesin motors carry vesicles and mitochondria away from the cell body. In cross-section they look like small hollow rings.

Dendritic microtubules are hollow tubes of α- and β-tubulin, about 25 nm wide, that support the dendrite and act as tracks for transport within it. Unlike those in the axon, they have mixed polarity, so motor proteins carry cargo in both directions, and they only occasionally extend into the spines. In cross-section they look like hollow rings, much as axonal microtubules do.

Spine actin is the filamentous actin (F-actin) network inside a dendritic spine, made of two strands of globular actin subunits twisted into a helix. This meshwork is concentrated in the spine head, where it gives the spine its shape and drives the size changes that accompany strengthening or weakening of the synapse. Each filament is only about 7 nm across, which makes the meshwork hard to pick out on ordinary electron micrographs.

keys: Synapse: vesicles near the active zone
parts.description: Synaptic vesicles near the active zone, the specialised release site on the presynaptic membrane, are small membrane-bound sacs that store glutamate. They form the readily releasable pool, the vesicles ready to fuse at once. Each vesicle is about 40 to 50 nm across and can fuse rapidly with the membrane when calcium enters the terminal. In an electron micrograph they appear as small, clear, round profiles clustered at the release site.

keys: Synapse: vesicles deeper in the bouton
parts.description: Synaptic vesicles deeper in the axon terminal form the reserve pool, small membrane-bound sacs filled with glutamate that lie away from the active zone. Synapsin, a protein that tethers them to the actin cytoskeleton, holds them in place, and they move to the release site during sustained, high-frequency firing. In an electron micrograph they are the clear round profiles scattered through the terminal, away from the membrane.

keys: Synapse: vesicles cut by the section
parts.description: Synaptic vesicles are small membrane-bound spheres in the axon terminal that store neurotransmitter, about 40 to 50 nm across. Because a thin section of tissue may pass through a vesicle off-centre, many vesicle profiles look smaller than their true diameter. Their clear, round, fairly uniform appearance is what identifies them in an electron micrograph.

keys: Synapse: cut edges of the vesicles
parts.description: The synaptic vesicle membrane is the lipid bilayer wall of each vesicle, and it carries the proteins that load and recycle the transmitter. Among them are the vesicular glutamate transporter (VGLUT), which pumps glutamate into the vesicle, and a proton pump (V-ATPase) that creates the proton gradient VGLUT uses. After release, this membrane is retrieved from the cell surface by endocytosis and reused.

The membrane of a docked vesicle is the vesicle wall at the point where it touches the presynaptic membrane, and it carries synaptobrevin-2 (VAMP2), one of the SNARE proteins that drive fusion. Synaptobrevin-2 zips together with syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25 on the presynaptic membrane, pulling the two membranes into close contact. When calcium arrives, synaptotagmin-1 triggers this zipper to complete fusion.

A docked vesicle is a synaptic vesicle attached directly to the presynaptic membrane at the active zone, with no visible gap between the two membranes. It is primed and ready to fuse, so when calcium enters the terminal it can release its glutamate into the synaptic cleft almost at once. In an electron micrograph docked vesicles look like small clear circles pressed against the dark presynaptic membrane.

Vesicle tethers are short protein filaments that link synaptic vesicles to the active zone scaffold and hold them in place before they dock. They include RIM, a scaffold protein that binds the vesicle protein Rab3, along with the large active-zone proteins bassoon and piccolo. In an electron micrograph the tethers show as thin filaments stretching between the vesicle and the dense active-zone material.

Glutamate is an amino acid that acts as the main fast excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain, and it is stored inside synaptic vesicles until release. When a vesicle fuses, glutamate diffuses into the synaptic cleft and binds AMPA and NMDA receptors on the postsynaptic side. It is then removed from the cleft by transporters, mainly on nearby astrocytes, which ends the signal.

Active zone densities are the dark, electron-dense protein scaffolds on the inner face of the presynaptic membrane, where vesicles dock and release. They are built from proteins such as bassoon, piccolo, RIM and Munc13, which organise vesicle docking and line up release sites opposite the postsynaptic receptors. In an electron micrograph they appear as dark projections rising from the presynaptic membrane.
